title: The Problem With Group Chats
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko argues that parents who keep their children off Instagram and Snapchat often grant WhatsApp-style group chats as a consolation prize without seeing that they are a form of social media in their own right. Prompted by Sophie Winkleman's warning that children need protection from each other in big virtual groups, she draws on another mother's experience, American Academy of Pediatrics commentary and her own 14-year-old son's chat to show how the herd dynamic produces profanity, pile-ons, inappropriate images and a relentless volume of notifications. She adds that group chats create easy, nearly invisible exclusion, and that preteens lack the impulse control and perspective-taking to handle them. Her conclusion is simple and parental: no group chats for preteens, with one-on-one messaging or calls as the alternative and one-way team chats as the exception. She frames this as part of a parent's job to be the child's prefrontal cortex until it develops.
points: Group chats are a risk category of their own, because the herd mentality changes how kids behave: a boy who was clean in one-on-one texts became profane and cruel in the group.

Meanness spreads contagiously in group settings, since status-sensitive kids find it easier to pile on than to dissent, and the AAP-cited research says teens conform more readily to aggressive messages than to friendly ones.
Even harmless chats carry an opportunity cost, because constant pinging (one girl received 1,084 unread messages in a school day) pulls attention away from real-world activity.
Group chats make exclusion trivial, as the 'silent exclusion' example of a secret sleepover chat shows, and over half of 13- to 17-year-olds report being left out of one.
The practical rule is no group chats before high school, offering direct messages or calls instead and requesting one-way chats when a team or club needs to share information.
quotes: The more I read and think about group chats, the more convinced I am that parents should not allow any preteen to participate in them.
Anywhere a herd can collect is a very bad idea, I think, for children. It’s not safe… Children themselves have to be protected from each other. They shouldn’t be in big virtual groups.

Unfortunately, it’s easier to be mean when it feels like you’re just typing into a phone, instead of speaking directly to another person and being forced to confront the emotional impact of your words, only to see the hurt or disappointment spreading across their face.
Meanness has a contagious effect in group chats, with kids piling on as soon as one person makes an unkind or backhanded observation about someone else.

Kids this age are impulsive; they need to be protected from their own instincts, at least temporarily. To use NYU professor Scott Galloway’s great line, “My job is to be their prefrontal cortex before it shows up.” That is every parent’s job, whether we like it or not.
Even if group chats were harmless, the sheer volume of messages that many kids receive on a daily basis should be grounds for a ban.
I think it’s fairly simple. No group chats. Tell your preteen kid that, like social media, it’s just not something you do as a family, especially not before high school.

Assure them that you’re not cutting them off from friends or depriving them of important information; rather, you’re trying to extract them from an unhealthy social environment that wastes time, sows drama, and makes them behave in less-than-ideal ways.
